reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: A congenital vascular malformation historically termed verrucous haemangioma, now recognised as a venous malformation with a hyperkeratotic (warty) surface
Typically presents as a bluish-red plaque or cluster of lesions, most often on a lower limb, that becomes progressively verrucous and hyperkeratotic over time
Unlike infantile haemangioma it does not involute and it is GLUT1-negative, though older confusing nomenclature persists
It tends to enlarge with growth of the child and may bleed, become crusted or secondarily infected
Somatic activating variants in MAP3K3 have been identified, distinguishing it molecularly from common venous malformations
Histology shows dilated venous channels in the dermis and subcutis with overlying epidermal hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis
The deep component often extends beyond the visible surface, which explains the tendency to recur after superficial treatment
Management is guided by symptoms and includes complete surgical excision where feasible, with laser or other modalities for selected lesions
reference.pathophysiology: Verrucous venous malformation is a congenital slow-flow venous malformation in which dilated, abnormal venous channels occupy the dermis and subcutis while the overlying epidermis develops reactive hyperkeratosis, acanthosis and papillomatosis, giving the characteristic warty surface. Somatic activating variants in MAP3K3 drive the lesion and separate it molecularly from common venous malformations. Because the malformed vessels frequently extend deeper than the visible verrucous surface, superficial or incomplete treatment tends to be followed by recurrence and progressive enlargement.
additionalDifferentials: Pyogenic granuloma or other bleeding vascular lesion
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination documenting the verrucous, hyperkeratotic surface and distribution
MRI to assess the depth and full extent of the venous component
Doppler ultrasound to confirm slow-flow venous characteristics
Histopathology showing dermal venous channels with epidermal hyperkeratosis
GLUT1 immunostaining to exclude infantile haemangioma
Molecular testing for MAP3K3 variants where available
redFlags: Recurrent or significant bleeding from the lesion
Functional impairment when overlying joints or weight-bearing areas
Diagnostic uncertainty raising concern for another lesion
reference.prognosis: Verrucous venous malformation is benign but persistent and does not involute; it commonly enlarges with the patient and is prone to recurrence after incomplete treatment, so wide complete excision offers the best chance of durable control while symptoms otherwise guide conservative management.
pitfalls: Treating it as an involuting infantile haemangioma and awaiting spontaneous resolution
Underestimating the deep venous component and performing inadequate superficial excision
Relying on the outdated term verrucous haemangioma and misclassifying it as a tumour
Overlooking bleeding and infection risk in hyperkeratotic, friable lesions
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
